title: Class 5 Maths Boxes and Sketches: Nets, 3D Shapes & Case Studies + Free Quiz
meta_title: Class 5 Maths Boxes and Sketches: Nets & 3D Guide
meta_desc: Class 5 maths boxes and sketches made simple: fold nets into cubes and cuboids, match a net to its solid, read deep drawings, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: NCERT Class 5 Chapter 9 is really about flattening a box and folding it back. Here is how nets, cube and cuboid faces, and deep drawings fit together, with a worked packaging case study and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a child an empty toothpaste carton and ask them to cut along the edges and flatten it out. What lands on the table is a strange plus-shaped or T-shaped flat figure — and that figure is the whole point of class 5 maths boxes and sketches. NCERT Chapter 9 takes children from solid boxes they can hold to the flat ‘nets’ those boxes come from, and back again. It is one of the few chapters where the maths is literally sitting in the kitchen cupboard.

Most kids find it fun until they hit the tricky bit: looking at a flat net and picturing the box it folds into without actually folding it. That mental folding is the skill this chapter builds. Let me walk through how the ideas connect, then work through a real packaging case study of the kind the exam loves.

What the ‘boxes and sketches’ chapter is really about

Strip away the pictures and Chapter 9 covers three linked ideas: solids and their faces, nets that fold into those solids, and deep drawings (3D sketches) that let you show a box on flat paper. A child who gets all three can look at a carton and answer ‘how many faces, how many corners, and what would it look like opened out?’ without hesitating.

The two solids that matter most here are the cube and the cuboid, because almost every box in real life is one of them.

  • Face — a flat surface of the box. A cube and a cuboid both have 6.
  • Edge — the line where two faces meet. Both have 12.
  • Corner (vertex) — where edges meet. Both have 8.
  • Net — the flat shape you get by opening a box out along its edges.

Nets: the flat shape that folds into a box

A net is a box unfolded. The key rule for Chapter 9: a cube always opens into 6 squares joined edge to edge, and a cuboid opens into 6 rectangles (with opposite faces matching in size). But — and this is where children slip — not every arrangement of 6 squares folds back into a cube. There are exactly 11 different nets that work for a cube. Some arrangements leave two faces overlapping and cannot close up.

The honest trick I give students: do not try to memorise all 11 nets. Instead, pick the square that will be the base, then mentally fold the four squares around it up as walls, and check whether the last square can become a lid without clashing. If two squares would land on the same spot, it is not a valid net.

Matching a net to its solid

Exam questions often show one net and four solids (or one solid and four nets) and ask which pair belongs together. Count first, fold second. If the net has 6 equal squares, the solid must be a cube; if it has rectangles, it is a cuboid; a triangle in the net means it is not a box at all.

Reading a deep drawing (3D sketch)

NCERT calls a 3D sketch a ‘deep drawing’ — a way of drawing a box on flat paper so it still looks solid. The trick artists use is simple: draw the front face square-on, then push slanting lines back at an angle for the depth, and only some edges stay hidden. A deep drawing lets you show length, width and height all at once.

A quick classroom test of understanding: ask how many faces you can actually see in a deep drawing of a cube. The answer is at most three — front, top and one side. The other three are hidden behind. Children who realise a drawing can only ever show three faces of a box stop drawing impossible pictures.

Case study: the sweet-box maker

Here is the kind of passage the case-study book uses. Read it, then try the questions before checking the working.

Meena runs a small mithai shop in Nagpur. She buys flat cardboard nets and folds them into boxes. Today she has nets that are each made of 6 equal squares, every square measuring 10 cm by 10 cm. She folded 40 boxes for Diwali orders.

Question 1: What solid does each net fold into?

Six equal squares folding into a closed box can only make a cube. Rectangles would give a cuboid; equal squares give a cube.

Question 2: How many corners and edges does each finished box have?

Every cube has 8 corners and 12 edges, no matter its size. The 10 cm measurement does not change these counts — a common trap in the exam.

Question 3: How many square faces did Meena fold in total?

Each box uses 6 squares, and she made 40 boxes: 6 × 40 = 240 squares. Notice the question is about faces, not boxes — read carefully.

That last step is why these case studies are worth practising. The maths is easy; the reading is where marks are won or lost. The full solutions book walks through dozens of passages like Meena’s, each with the working shown line by line.

A simple home activity that beats any worksheet

Before the quiz, one thing worth doing this week: save three empty boxes — a matchbox, a dice, and a cereal carton. Cut each along the edges, lay the net flat, and count the faces. Then have your child draw a deep drawing of each. Ten minutes of real cardboard teaches more than an hour of pictures, because the folding happens in their hands instead of only in their head.

quiz.title: Class 5 Boxes and Sketches Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on faces, edges, corners, nets and deep drawings from NCERT Chapter 9. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 5 Maths Chapter 9: Boxes and Sketches

questions.q: How many faces does a cube have?
questions.explanation: A cube has 6 flat square faces — top, bottom and four sides.

questions.q: A net that folds into a cube is made of how many equal squares?
questions.explanation: A cube opens out into 6 equal squares joined edge to edge.

questions.q: Which solid has 6 faces that are all rectangles?
questions.explanation: A cuboid, like a toothpaste carton, has 6 rectangular faces with opposite faces matching.

questions.q: How many edges does a cube have?
questions.explanation: A cube has 12 edges, the lines where two faces meet.

questions.q: How many corners (vertices) does a cuboid have?
questions.explanation: A cuboid has 8 corners, the same as a cube.

questions.q: Which of these is a 3D shape (a solid), not a flat shape?
questions.explanation: A cube is a solid you can hold. A square, rectangle and triangle are flat shapes.

questions.q: In a deep drawing of a cube, at most how many faces can you see?
questions.explanation: A deep drawing shows at most 3 faces — front, top and one side. The other three are hidden.

questions.q: A net is made of 3 rectangles and 2 circles. What solid does it fold into?
questions.explanation: Two circles for the top and bottom and a rectangle that curves round make a cylinder, like a tin.

faq.q: What is NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 9 about?
faq.a: It is called Boxes and Sketches. Children learn about solids like cubes and cuboids, the flat nets those boxes fold from, and deep drawings that show a box in 3D on flat paper.

faq.q: What is a net in the boxes and sketches chapter?
faq.a: A net is a box opened out flat along its edges. A cube gives a net of 6 equal squares; a cuboid gives 6 rectangles. Folding the net back up rebuilds the box.

faq.q: How do you match a net to its solid?
faq.a: Count the shapes first. Six equal squares means a cube, six rectangles means a cuboid, and two circles with a rectangle means a cylinder. Then mentally fold to confirm the faces meet without overlapping.
A deep drawing is NCERT’s name for a 3D sketch — a way to draw a box so it looks solid, showing length, width and height together. You can see at most three faces of a box in one.
